L30: 
L31: OutputBuffer is of type FILE_ID_INFORMATION as specified in 【4†[MS-FSCC]】 section 【5†2.4.26】.
L32: 
L33: Pseudocode for the operation is as follows:
L34: 
L35:   * If OutputBufferSize is smaller than sizeof(FILE_ID_INFORMATION), the operation MUST be failed with STATUS_INFO_LENGTH_MISMATCH.
L36: 
L37:   * OutputBuffer MUST be constructed as follows:
L38: 
L39:     * OutputBuffer.VolumeSerialNumber set to Open.File.Volume.VolumeSerialNumber.
L40: 
L41:     * OutBuffer.FileId set to Open.File.FileId128.
L42:   * Upon successful completion of the operation, the object store MUST return:
L43: 
L44:     * ByteCount set to sizeof(FILE_ID_INFORMATION)
L45: 
L46:     * Status set to STATUS_SUCCESS.

L24: # 2.1.5.12.5 FileAttributeTagInformation
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: OutputBuffer is of type FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TAG_INFORMATION as defined in 【4†[MS-FSCC]】 section 【5†2.4.6】.
L32: 
L33: Pseudocode for the operation is as follows:
L34: 
L35:   * If OutputBufferSize is smaller than sizeof(FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TAG_INFORMATION), the operation MUST be failed with STATUS_INFO_LENGTH_MISMATCH.
L36: 
L37:   * If Open.GrantedAccess does not contain FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES, the operation MUST be failed with STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED.
L38: 
L39:   * If Open.Stream.StreamType is DirectoryStream:
L40:     * The object store MUST set OutputBuffer.FileAttributes equal to the value of Open.File.FileAttributes.
L41: 
L42:     * The object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L43: 
L44:   * Else:
L45:     * This is a DataStream. The object store MUST set OutputBuffer.FileAttributes equal to the value of Open.File.FileAttributes. The following attribute values, if they are set in Open.File.FileAttributes, MUST NOT be copied to OutputBuffer.FileAttributes (attribute flags are defined in [MS-FSCC] section 【6†2.6】):
L46: 
L47:       * FILE_ATTRIBUTE_COMPRESSED
L48: 
L49:       * FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY
L50: 
L51:       * FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SPARSE_FILE
L52: 
L53:       * FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ENCRYPTED
L54: 
L55:       * FILE_ATTRIBUTE_INTEGRITY_STREAM【7†<159>】
L56:     * If Open.Stream.IsSparse is TRUE, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SPARSE_FILE in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L57: 
L58:     * If Open.Stream.IsEncrypted is TRUE, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ENCRYPTED in OuputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L59: 
L60:     * If Open.Stream.IsTemporary is TRUE, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L61: 
L62:     * If Open.Stream.IsCompressed is TRUE, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_COMPRESSED in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L63:     * If Open.Stream.ChecksumAlgorithm != CHECKSUM_TYPE_NONE, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_INTEGRITY_STREAM in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.【8†<160>】
L64: 
L65:   * EndIf
L66: 
L67:   * If OutputBuffer.FileAttributes is 0, the object store MUST set FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL in OutputBuffer.FileAttributes.
L68: 
L69:   * OutputBuffer.ReparseTag MUST be set to Open.File.ReparseTag.
L70: 
L71:   * Upon successful completion of the operation, the object store MUST return:
L72: 
L73:     * ByteCount set to sizeof(FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TAG_INFORMATION).
L74:     * Status set to STATUS_SUCCESS.

L24: # FILE_ID_INFO structure (winbase.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Contains identification information for a file. This structure is returned from the 【5†GetFileInformationByHandleEx】 function when FileIdInfo is passed in the FileInformationClass parameter.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `typedef struct _FILE_ID_INFO {
L37:       ULONGLONG   VolumeSerialNumber;
L38:       FILE_ID_128 FileId;
L39:     } FILE_ID_INFO, *PFILE_ID_INFO;
L40:     `
L41: ## Members
L42: 
L43: `VolumeSerialNumber`
L44: 
L45: The serial number of the volume that contains a file.
L46: 
L47: `FileId`
L48: 
L49: The 128-bit file identifier for the file. The file identifier and the volume serial number uniquely identify a file on a single computer. To determine whether two open handles represent the same file, combine the identifier and the volume serial number for each file and compare them.
L50: ## Requirements
L51: 
L52: Requirement  | Value
L53: --- | ---
L54: Minimum supported client  | None supported
L55: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2012 [desktop apps only]
L56: Header  | winbase.h (include Windows.h)
L57:

L24: # CreateRestrictedToken function (securitybaseapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The CreateRestrictedToken function creates a new 【5†access token】 that is a restricted version of an existing access token. The restricted token can have disabled 【6†security identifiers】 (SIDs), deleted privileges, and a list of restricting SIDs. For more information, see 【7†Restricted Tokens】.
L33: ## Syntax
L34: 
L35:     `BOOL CreateRestrictedToken(
L36:       [in]           HANDLE               ExistingTokenHandle,
L37:       [in]           DWORD                Flags,
L38:       [in]           DWORD                DisableSidCount,
L39:       [in, optional] PSID_AND_ATTRIBUTES  SidsToDisable,
L40:       [in]           DWORD                DeletePrivilegeCount,
L41:       [in, optional] PLUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES PrivilegesToDelete,
L42:       [in]           DWORD                RestrictedSidCount,
L43:       [in, optional] PSID_AND_ATTRIBUTES  SidsToRestrict,
L44:       [out]          PHANDLE              NewTokenHandle
L45:     );
L46:     `
L47: ## Parameters
L48: 
L49: `[in] ExistingTokenHandle`
L50: 
L51: A handle to a 【8†primary】 or 【9†impersonation token】. The token can also be a restricted token. The handle must have TOKEN_DUPLICATE access to the token.
L52: 
L53: `[in] Flags`
L54: 
L55: Specifies additional privilege options. This parameter can be zero or a combination of the following values.
L56: Value  | Meaning
L57: --- | ---
L58: DISABLE_MAX_PRIVILEGE
L59: `0x1`  | Disables all privileges in the new token except the SeChangeNotifyPrivilege privilege. If this value is specified, the DeletePrivilegeCount and PrivilegesToDelete parameters are ignored.
L60: SANDBOX_INERT
L61: `0x2`  | If this value is used, the system does not check 【10†AppLocker】 rules or apply 【11†Software Restriction Policies】. For 【10†AppLocker】, this flag disables checks for all four rule collections: Executable, Windows Installer, Script, and DLL.
L62: When creating a setup program that must run extracted DLLs during installation, use the flag SAFER_TOKEN_MAKE_INERT in the 【12†SaferComputeTokenFromLevel】 function.
L63: A token can be queried for existence of this flag by using 【13†GetTokenInformation】.
L64: Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows 7, Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: On systems with KB2532445 installed, the caller must be running as LocalSystem or TrustedInstaller or the system ignores this flag. For more information, see 【14†You can circumvent AppLocker rules by using an Office macro on a computer that is running Windows 7 or Windows Server 2008 R2†support.microsoft.com】.
L65: Windows Server 2008, Windows Vista, Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: AppLocker is not supported. AppLocker was introduced in Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2.
L66: LUA_TOKEN
L67: `0x4`  | The new token is a LUA token.
L68: Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP: This value is not supported.
L69: WRITE_RESTRICTED
L70: `0x8`  | The new token contains restricting SIDs that are considered only when evaluating write access.
L71: Windows XP with SP2 and later: The value of this constant is `0x4`. For an application to be compatible with Windows XP with SP2 and later operating systems, the application should query the operating system by calling the 【15†GetVersionEx】 function to determine which value should be used.
L72: Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP with SP1 and earlier: This value is not supported.
L73: `[in] DisableSidCount`
L74: 
L75: Specifies the number of entries in the SidsToDisable array.
L76: 
L77: `[in, optional] SidsToDisable`
L78: 
L79: A pointer to an array of 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify the deny-only SIDs in the restricted token. The system uses a deny-only SID to deny access to a securable object. The absence of a deny-only SID does not allow access.
L80: 
L81: Disabling a SID turns on SE_GROUP_USE_FOR_DENY_ONLY and turns off SE_GROUP_ENABLED and SE_GROUP_ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT. All other attributes are ignored.
L82: Deny-only attributes apply to any combination of an existing token's SIDs, including the user SID and group SIDs that have the SE_GROUP_MANDATORY attribute. To get the SIDs associated with the existing token, use the 【13†GetTokenInformation】 function with the TokenUser and TokenGroups flags. The function ignores any SIDs in the array that are not also found in the existing token.
L83: 
L84: The function ignores the Attributes member of the 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structure.
L85: This parameter can be NULL if no SIDs are to be disabled.
L86: 
L87: `[in] DeletePrivilegeCount`
L88: 
L89: Specifies the number of entries in the PrivilegesToDelete array.
L90: 
L91: `[in, optional] PrivilegesToDelete`
L92: 
L93: A pointer to an array of 【17†LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify the privileges to delete in the restricted token.
L94: The 【13†GetTokenInformation】 function can be used with the TokenPrivileges flag to retrieve the privileges held by the existing token. The function ignores any privileges in the array that are not held by the existing token.
L95: 
L96: The function ignores the Attributes members of the 【17†LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures.
L97: 
L98: This parameter can be NULL if you do not want to delete any privileges.
L99: 
L100: If the calling program passes too many privileges in this array, CreateRestrictedToken returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER.
L101: `[in] RestrictedSidCount`
L102: 
L103: Specifies the number of entries in the SidsToRestrict array.
L104: 
L105: `[in, optional] SidsToRestrict`
L106: A pointer to an array of 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structures that specify a list of restricting SIDs for the new token. If the existing token is a restricted token, the list of restricting SIDs for the new token is the intersection of this array and the list of restricting SIDs for the existing token. No check is performed to remove duplicate SIDs that were placed on the SidsToRestrict parameter. Duplicate SIDs allow a restricted token to have redundant information in the restricting SID list.
L107: The Attributes member of the 【16†SID_AND_ATTRIBUTES】 structure must be zero. Restricting SIDs are always enabled for access checks.
L108: 
L109: This parameter can be NULL if you do not want to specify any restricting SIDs.
L110: 
L111: `[out] NewTokenHandle`
L112: A pointer to a variable that receives a handle to the new restricted token. This handle has the same access rights as ExistingTokenHandle. The new token is the same type, 【8†primary】 or 【9†impersonation】, as the existing token. The handle returned in NewTokenHandle can be duplicated.
L113: ## Return value
L114: 
L115: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L116: 
L117: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call 【18†GetLastError】.
L118: ## Remarks
L119: 
L120: The CreateRestrictedToken function can restrict the token in the following ways:
L121:   * Apply the deny-only attribute to SIDs in the token so they cannot be used to access secured objects. For more information about the deny-only attribute, see 【19†SID Attributes in an Access Token】.
L122:   * Remove 【20†privileges】 from the token.
L123:   * Specify a list of restricting SIDs, which the system uses when it checks the token's access to a securable object. The system performs two access checks: one using the token's enabled SIDs, and another using the list of restricting SIDs. Access is granted only if both access checks allow the requested access rights.
L124: You can use the restricted token in the 【21†CreateProcessAsUser】 function to create a process that has restricted access rights and privileges. If a process calls CreateProcessAsUser using a restricted version of its own token, the calling process does not need to have the SE_ASSIGNPRIMARYTOKEN_NAME privilege.
L125: 
L126: You can use the restricted token in the 【22†ImpersonateLoggedOnUser】 function.
L127: 
L128: Warning
L129: Applications that use restricted tokens should run the restricted application on desktops other than the default desktop. This is necessary to prevent an attack by a restricted application, using SendMessage or PostMessage, to unrestricted applications on the default desktop. If necessary, switch between desktops for your application purposes.
L130: ## Requirements
L131: 
L132: Requirement  | Value
L133: --- | ---
L134: Minimum supported client  | Windows XP [desktop apps only]
L135: Minimum supported server  | Windows Server 2003 [desktop apps only]
L136: Target Platform  | Windows
L137: Header  | securitybaseapi.h (include Windows.h)
L138: Library  | Advapi32.lib
L139: DLL  | Advapi32.dll

L24: # ImpersonateLoggedOnUser function (securitybaseapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The ImpersonateLoggedOnUser function lets the calling thread impersonate the 【5†security context】 of a logged-on user. The user is represented by a token handle.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `BOOL ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(
L37:       [in] HANDLE hToken
L38:     );
L39:     `
L40: ## Parameters
L41: 
L42: `[in] hToken`
L43: A handle to a primary or impersonation 【6†access token】 that represents a logged-on user. This can be a token handle returned by a call to 【7†LogonUser】, 【8†CreateRestrictedToken】, 【9†DuplicateToken】, 【10†DuplicateTokenEx】, 【11†OpenProcessToken】, or 【12†OpenThreadToken】 functions. If hToken is a handle to a 【13†primary token】, the token must have TOKEN_QUERY and TOKEN_DUPLICATE access. If hToken is a handle to an 【14†impersonation token】, the token must have TOKEN_QUERY and TOKEN_IMPERSONATE access.
L44: ## Return value
L45: 
L46: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L47: 
L48: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call 【15†GetLastError】.
L49: ## Remarks
L50: 
L51: The impersonation lasts until the thread exits or until it calls 【16†RevertToSelf】.
L52: 
L53: The calling thread does not need to have any particular 【13†privileges】 to call ImpersonateLoggedOnUser.
L54: If the call to ImpersonateLoggedOnUser fails, the client connection is not impersonated and the client request is made in the security context of the process. If the process is running as a highly privileged account, such as LocalSystem, or as a member of an administrative group, the user may be able to perform actions they would otherwise be disallowed.
L55: Therefore, it is important to always check the return value of the call, and if it fails, raise an error; do not continue execution of the client request.
L56: All impersonate functions, including ImpersonateLoggedOnUser allow the requested impersonation if one of the following is true:
L57: 
L58:   * The caller has the SeImpersonatePrivilege privilege.
L59:   * A process (or another process in the caller's logon session) created the token using explicit credentials through 【7†LogonUser】 or 【17†LsaLogonUser】 function.
L60:   * The authenticated identity is same as the caller.
L61: 
L62: Important
L63: The token must have an impersonation level of SecurityImpersonation or higher for impersonation to succeed. Tokens with SecurityIdentification or SecurityAnonymous levels cannot be used for impersonation, even if the caller has SeImpersonatePrivilege. SecurityIdentification tokens allow identity verification and ACL checks but do not permit impersonation.
L64: #### Impersonation Level Requirements
L65: 
L66: The behavior varies based on the token's impersonation level:
L67:   * SecurityAnonymous: The server cannot obtain client identity information and cannot impersonate the client.
L68:   * SecurityIdentification: The server can obtain the client's identity and perform access validation, but cannot impersonate the client. This is the default level for many scenarios.
L69:   * SecurityImpersonation: The server can impersonate the client's security context on the local system. This is the minimum level required for ImpersonateLoggedOnUser to succeed.
L70:   * SecurityDelegation: The server can impersonate the client on remote systems as well as locally.
L71: Windows XP with SP1 and earlier: The SeImpersonatePrivilege privilege is not supported.
L72: 
L73: For more information about impersonation, see 【18†Client Impersonation】.

L24: # RevertToSelf function (securitybaseapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: The RevertToSelf function terminates the impersonation of a client application.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `BOOL RevertToSelf();
L37:     `
L38: 
L39: ## Return value
L40: 
L41: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero.
L42: 
L43: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call 【5†GetLastError】.
L44: ## Remarks
L45: 
L46: A 【6†process】 should call the RevertToSelf function after finishing any impersonation begun by using the 【7†DdeImpersonateClient】, 【8†ImpersonateDdeClientWindow】, 【9†ImpersonateLoggedOnUser】, 【10†ImpersonateNamedPipeClient】, 【11†ImpersonateSelf】, 【12†ImpersonateAnonymousToken】 or 【13†SetThreadToken】 function.
L47: 
L48: An RPC server that used the 【14†RpcImpersonateClient】 function to impersonate a client must call the 【15†RpcRevertToSelf】 or 【16†RpcRevertToSelfEx】 to end the impersonation.
L49: If RevertToSelf fails, your application continues to run in the context of the client, which is not appropriate. You should shut down the process if RevertToSelf fails.
L50: #### Examples
L51: 
L52: For an example that uses this function, see 【17†Verifying Client Access with ACLs】.

L24: # CreateFileW function (fileapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: ## In this article
L30: 
L31: Creates or opens a file or I/O device. The most commonly used I/O devices are as follows: file, file stream, directory, physical disk, volume, console buffer, tape drive, communications resource, mailslot, and pipe. The function returns a handle that can be used to access the file or device for various types of I/O depending on the file or device and the flags and attributes specified.
L32: To perform this operation as a transacted operation, which results in a handle that can be used for transacted I/O, use the 【5†CreateFileTransacted】 function.
L33: ## Syntax
L34: 
L35:     `HANDLE CreateFileW(
L36:       [in]           LPCWSTR               lpFileName,
L37:       [in]           DWORD                 dwDesiredAccess,
L38:       [in]           DWORD                 dwShareMode,
L39:       [in, optional] LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpSecurityAttributes,
L40:       [in]           DWORD                 dwCreationDisposition,
L41:       [in]           DWORD                 dwFlagsAndAttributes,
L42:       [in, optional] HANDLE                hTemplateFile
L43:     );
L44:     `
L45: ## Parameters
L46: 
L47: `[in] lpFileName`
L48: 
L49: The name of the file or device to be created or opened. You may use either forward slashes (/) or backslashes (\) in this name.
L50: 
L51: For information on special device names, see 【6†Defining an MS-DOS Device Name】.
L52: 
L53: To create a file stream, specify the name of the file, a colon, and then the name of the stream. For more information, see 【7†File Streams】.
L54: By default, the name is limited to MAX_PATH characters. To extend this limit to 32,767 wide characters, prepend "\\?\" to the path. For more information, see 【8†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】.
L55: 
L56: Tip
L57: 
L58: Starting with Windows 10, Version 1607, you can opt-in to remove the MAX_PATH limitation without prepending "\\?\". See the "Maximum Path Length Limitation" section of 【8†Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces】 for details.
L59: 
L60: `[in] dwDesiredAccess`
L61: The requested access to the file or device, which can be summarized as read, write, both or neither zero).
L62: 
L63: The most commonly used values are GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE, or both (`GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE`). For more information, see 【9†Generic Access Rights】, 【10†File Security and Access Rights】, 【11†File Access Rights Constants】, and 【12†ACCESS_MASK】.
L64: If this parameter is zero, the application can query certain metadata such as file, directory, or device attributes without accessing that file or device, even if GENERIC_READ access would have been denied.
L65: 
L66: You cannot request an access mode that conflicts with the sharing mode that is specified by the dwShareMode parameter in an open request that already has an open handle.
L67: 
L68: For more information, see the Remarks section of this topic and 【13†Creating and Opening Files】.
L69: 
L70: `[in] dwShareMode`
L71: The requested sharing mode of the file or device, which can be read, write, both, delete, all of these, or none (refer to the following table). Access requests to attributes or extended attributes are not affected by this flag.
L72: 
L73: If this parameter is zero and CreateFile succeeds, the file or device cannot be shared and cannot be opened again until the handle to the file or device is closed. For more information, see the Remarks section.
L74: You cannot request a sharing mode that conflicts with the access mode that is specified in an existing request that has an open handle. CreateFile would fail and the 【14†GetLastError】 function would return ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION.
L75: To enable a process to share a file or device while another process has the file or device open, use a compatible combination of one or more of the following values. For more information about valid combinations of this parameter with the dwDesiredAccess parameter, see 【13†Creating and Opening Files】.
L76: 
L77: Note The sharing options for each open handle remain in effect until that handle is closed, regardless of process context.
L78: 
L79: Value  | Meaning
L80: --- | ---
L81: 0
L82: 0x00000000
L83:  | Prevents subsequent open operations on a file or device if they request delete, read, or write access.
L84: 
L85: FILE_SHARE_DELETE
L86: 0x00000004
L87:  | Enables subsequent open operations on a file or device to request delete access. Otherwise, no process can open the file or device if it requests delete access. If this flag is not specified, but the file or device has been opened for delete access, the function fails. Note Delete access allows both delete and rename operations.
L88: FILE_SHARE_READ
L89: 0x00000001
L90:  | Enables subsequent open operations on a file or device to request read access. Otherwise, no process can open the file or device if it requests read access. If this flag is not specified, but the file or device has been opened for read access, the function fails.
L91: FILE_SHARE_WRITE
L92: 0x00000002
L93:  | Enables subsequent open operations on a file or device to request write access. Otherwise, no process can open the file or device if it requests write access. If this flag is not specified, but the file or device has been opened for write access or has a file mapping with write access, the function fails.
L94: 
L95: `[in, optional] lpSecurityAttributes`
L96: A pointer to a 【15†SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES】 structure that contains two separate but related data members: an optional security descriptor, and a Boolean value that determines whether the returned handle can be inherited by child processes.
L97: 
L98: This parameter can be NULL.
L99: 
L100: If this parameter is NULL, the handle returned by CreateFile cannot be inherited by any child processes the application may create and the file or device associated with the returned handle gets a default security descriptor.
L101: The lpSecurityDescriptor member of the structure specifies a 【16†SECURITY_DESCRIPTOR】 for a file or device. If this member is NULL, the file or device associated with the returned handle is assigned a default security descriptor.
L102: 
L103: CreateFile ignores the lpSecurityDescriptor member when opening an existing file or device, but continues to use the bInheritHandle member.
L104: 
L105: The bInheritHandle member of the structure specifies whether the returned handle can be inherited.
L106: For more information, see the Remarks section.
L107: 
L108: `[in] dwCreationDisposition`
L109: 
L110: An action to take on a file or device that exists or does not exist.
L111: 
L112: For devices other than files, this parameter is usually set to OPEN_EXISTING.
L113: 
L114: For more information, see the Remarks section.
L115: 
L116: This parameter must be one of the following values, which cannot be combined:
L117: 
L118: Value  | Meaning
L119: --- | ---
L120: CREATE_ALWAYS
L121: 2
L122:  | Creates a new file, always. If the specified file exists and is writable, the function truncates the file, the function succeeds, and last-error code is set to ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS (183). If the specified file does not exist and is a valid path, a new file is created, the function succeeds, and the last-error code is set to zero. For more information, see the Remarks section of this topic.
L123: CREATE_NEW
L124: 1
L125:  | Creates a new file, only if it does not already exist. If the specified file exists, the function fails and the last-error code is set to ERROR_FILE_EXISTS (80). If the specified file does not exist and is a valid path to a writable location, a new file is created.
L126: OPEN_ALWAYS
L127: 4
L128:  | Opens a file, always. If the specified file exists, the function succeeds and the last-error code is set to ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS (183). If the specified file does not exist and is a valid path to a writable location, the function creates a file and the last-error code is set to zero.
L129: OPEN_EXISTING
L130: 3
L131:  | Opens a file or device, only if it exists. If the specified file or device does not exist, the function fails and the last-error code is set to ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (2). For more information about devices, see the Remarks section.
L132: TRUNCATE_EXISTING
L133: 5
L134:  | Opens a file and truncates it so that its size is zero bytes, only if it exists. If the specified file does not exist, the function fails and the last-error code is set to ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (2). The calling process must open the file with the GENERIC_WRITE bit set as part of the dwDesiredAccess parameter.
L135: 
L136: `[in] dwFlagsAndAttributes`
L137: 
L138: The file or device attributes and flags, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL being the most common default value for files.
L139: This parameter can include any combination of the available file attributes (FILE_ATTRIBUTE_*). All other file attributes override FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL.
L140: 
L141: This parameter can also contain combinations of flags (FILE_FLAG_) for control of file or device caching behavior, access modes, and other special-purpose flags. These combine with any FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ values.
L142: This parameter can also contain Security Quality of Service (SQOS) information by specifying the SECURITY_SQOS_PRESENT flag. Additional SQOS-related flags information is presented in the table following the attributes and flags tables.
L143: 
L144: Note When CreateFile opens an existing file, it generally combines the file flags with the file attributes of the existing file, and ignores any file attributes supplied as part of dwFlagsAndAttributes. Special cases are detailed in 【13†Creating and Opening Files】.
L145: Some of the following file attributes and flags may only apply to files and not necessarily all other types of devices that CreateFile can open. For additional information, see the Remarks section of this topic and 【13†Creating and Opening Files】.
L146: 
L147: For more advanced access to file attributes, see 【17†SetFileAttributes】. For a complete list of all file attributes with their values and descriptions, see 【18†File Attribute Constants】.
L148: 
L149: Attribute  | Meaning
L150: --- | ---
L151: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ARCHIVE
L152: 32 (0x20)
L153:  | The file should be archived. Applications use this attribute to mark files for backup or removal.
L154: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_ENCRYPTED
L155: 16384 (0x4000)
L156:  | The file or directory is encrypted. For a file, this means that all data in the file is encrypted. For a directory, this means that encryption is the default for newly created files and subdirectories. For more information, see 【19†File Encryption】. This flag has no effect if FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SYSTEM is also specified. This flag is not supported on Home, Home Premium, Starter, or ARM editions of Windows.
L157: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN
L158: 2 (0x2)
L159:  | The file is hidden. Do not include it in an ordinary directory listing.
L160: 
L161: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL
L162: 128 (0x80)
L163:  | The file does not have other attributes set. This attribute is valid only if used alone.
L164: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_OFFLINE
L165: 4096 (0x1000)
L166:  | The data of a file is not immediately available. This attribute indicates that file data is physically moved to offline storage. This attribute is used by Remote Storage, the hierarchical storage management software. Applications should not arbitrarily change this attribute.
L167: 
L168: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY
L169: 1 (0x1)
L170:  | The file is read only. Applications can read the file, but cannot write to or delete it.
L171: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_SYSTEM
L172: 4 (0x4)
L173:  | The file is part of or used exclusively by an operating system.
L174: 
L175: FILE_ATTRIBUTE_TEMPORARY
L176: 256 (0x100)
L177:  | The file is being used for temporary storage. For more information, see the 【20†Caching Behavior】 section of this topic.
L178: Flag  | Meaning
L179: --- | ---
L180: FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS
L181: 0x02000000
L182:  | The file is being opened or created for a backup or restore operation. The system ensures that the calling process overrides file security checks when the process has SE_BACKUP_NAME and SE_RESTORE_NAME privileges. For more information, see 【21†Changing Privileges in a Token】. You must set this flag to obtain a handle to a directory. A directory handle can be passed to some functions instead of a file handle. For more information, see the Remarks section.
L183: FILE_FLAG_DELETE_ON_CLOSE
L184: 0x04000000
L185:  | The file is to be deleted immediately after all of its handles are closed, which includes the specified handle and any other open or duplicated handles. If there are existing open handles to a file, the call fails unless they were all opened with the FILE_SHARE_DELETE share mode. Subsequent open requests for the file fail, unless the FILE_SHARE_DELETE share mode is specified.
L186: FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING
L187: 0x20000000
L188:  | The file or device is being opened with no system caching for data reads and writes. This flag does not affect hard disk caching or memory mapped files. There are strict requirements for successfully working with files opened with CreateFile using the FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING flag, for details see 【22†File Buffering】.
L189: FILE_FLAG_OPEN_NO_RECALL
L190: 0x00100000
L191:  | The file data is requested, but it should continue to be located in remote storage. It should not be transported back to local storage. This flag is for use by remote storage systems.
L192: FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT
L193: 0x00200000
L194:  | Normal 【23†reparse point】 processing will not occur; CreateFile will attempt to open the reparse point. When a file is opened, a file handle is returned, whether or not the filter that controls the reparse point is operational. This flag cannot be used with the CREATE_ALWAYS flag. If the file is not a reparse point, then this flag is ignored. For more information, see the Remarks section.
L195: FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED
L196: 0x40000000
L197:  | The file or device is being opened or created for asynchronous I/O. When subsequent I/O operations are completed on this handle, the event specified in the 【24†OVERLAPPED】 structure will be set to the signaled state. If this flag is specified, the file can be used for simultaneous read and write operations. If this flag is not specified, then I/O operations are serialized, even if the calls to the read and write functions specify an 【24†OVERLAPPED】 structure.
L198: For information about considerations when using a file handle created with this flag, see the 【25†Synchronous and Asynchronous I/O Handles】 section of this topic.
L199: FILE_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS
L200: 0x01000000
L201:  | Access will occur according to POSIX rules. This includes allowing multiple files with names, differing only in case, for file systems that support that naming. Use care when using this option, because files created with this flag may not be accessible by applications that are written for MS-DOS or 16-bit Windows.
L202: FILE_FLAG_RANDOM_ACCESS
L203: 0x10000000
